bib.title: IntellAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Conversational AI Systems

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 15 pages read (39,895 chars): body pp.1-8, references pp.9-10, appendix pp.11-15 (architecture figs, one worked example). References skimmed. The note's "Multi-turn evaluation" section (lines 374-393 of 06-evaluating-agents.md) was read too.

SOURCE: "IntellAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Conversational AI Systems". Elad Levi and Ilan Kadar, both at Plurai (Plurai is the only affiliation given). arXiv 2501.11067v1 [cs.CL], 19 Jan 2025. The PDF states no venue, so preprint. Code: github.com/plurai-ai/intellagent.

CORE CLAIM: Instead of the 50 airline and 115 retail hand-written tasks in τ-bench, build a graph of policies from the agent's system prompt. Random-walk it to sample many policy combinations at a controlled complexity, have an LLM write each scenario plus a matching database state, then run a simulated user against the agent and have an LLM critique the dialog policy by policy. The authors say this gives fine-grained, per-policy diagnostics, and that its model ranking agrees with τ-bench.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Pearson correlation between τ-bench and IntellAgent success rates is 0.98 for airline and 0.92 for retail. The setup is 6 models (claude-3.5-sonnet, gpt-4o, gemini-1.5-pro, gpt-4o-mini, claude-3.5-haiku, gemini-1.5-flash), each using native function calling with the τ-bench system prompt. The metric is success rate (Table 2, p.7). With n=6 points per environment, no interval is given, and the paper does not say whether runs were repeated.
2. IntellAgent produces 1,000 events per environment, at complexity levels 2 to 11, against τ-bench's 50 (airline) and 115 (retail) (p.7). The generator, user simulator and critique are all GPT-4o.
3. Absolute scores run much higher on IntellAgent than on τ-bench (Table 2). Airline: claude-3.5-sonnet 0.46 vs 0.70, gpt-4o 0.44 vs 0.70, gemini-1.5-flash 0.21 vs 0.40. Retail: claude-3.5-sonnet 0.69 vs 0.71, gpt-4o 0.51 vs 0.68. So the benchmark matches τ-bench's ranking but not its difficulty. The paper does not comment on this.
4. Success falls as complexity rises, at different rates per model (Fig. 2, p.7). Gemini-1.5-pro is clearly ahead of gpt-4o-mini in airline up to level 10, then the two converge. Only the top four models are plotted. No numbers are given in the text.
5. Model order changes by policy category (Fig. 3, p.8), and all models struggle with user-consent policies. The authors say τ-bench does not assess consent because it checks only the final database state.

QUOTES
- "Notably, this strong correlation persists despite IntellAgent being generated exclusively with synthetic data." (p.8)
- "The user has the option to terminate the interaction at any point, either when the chatbot successfully completes the task or if the chatbot fails to adhere to one of the policies and does not follow the expected behavior." (p.6)

LIMITS / NOT SHOWN
- The paper reports no human validation of the simulator, the critique, the generated events or the policy graph. Its only validation is the correlation with τ-bench, which is a ranking check, not a check of whether the judge is right.
- The same model, GPT-4o, generates the events, plays the user and judges, and GPT-4o is also one of the six agents under test. The paper does not discuss self-preference or bias.
- The user agent is told the expected chatbot behaviour at each step and can end the dialog early on a policy violation. This differs from τ-bench's hidden-info, progressive-disclosure user.
- The paper reports no repeated runs, no variance and no interval for the success rates. It gives no failure-rate figure for the critique, and does not say how often a dialog was resumed after the critique overruled the user agent.
- Edge weights (an LLM scores policy pairs 1-10 for how likely they are to co-occur) are not checked against real traffic. The authors list real conversation data as future work.
- Only two domains (airline, retail), both taken from τ-bench. It contains no ablation of the sampling strategy beyond a qualitative example (Table 1).
- It has no comparison with τ²-bench, personas or dual control. Models are 2024 models and have dated.
- The tone is promotional ("paradigm shift").

BUILDS ON: τ-bench (Yao et al., ref [33], 2024; its prompts, DB schemas and tools are reused). GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) is credited as inspiration for the policy graph. ALMITA (Arcadinho et al., 2024) and the LTM Benchmark (Castillo-Bolado et al., 2024) are the related conversational benchmarks. The authors' own earlier work is Intent-based prompt calibration (Levi et al., 2024). RAGAS (Es et al., 2023) appears in related work.

BEST-FIT SECTION: "Multi-turn evaluation", in the Simulated user bullet and the τ-bench paragraph. Note that the paper adds two things the note lacks.
(a) Scale and coverage: synthetic scenarios from a policy graph, with complexity as a controllable axis, and per-policy and per-complexity breakdowns instead of one pass rate.
(b) Per-policy critique of the dialog, catching things a final-DB-state check cannot, such as user consent.
It also gives the 0.98/0.92 rank agreement with τ-bench, which the note does not have. That is a small sharpens-or-adds item, and it needs the caveats above: n=6, same-family GPT-4o judge, no human audit.
It does not duplicate the note's GAUGE point, and it cuts the other way: IntellAgent uses a single cooperative simulator and still shows inflated absolute scores. The note's progressive-disclosure and τ² paragraphs are not touched by it. The paper never describes how the user agent discloses information.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 (p.2), the three-stage pipeline of event generation, dialog simulation and critique. Figure 2 (p.7) is the alternative: success against challenge level for the top four models. Table 2 (p.7) is the key table, and it is not a figure.

PROBLEMS: none. The text extracted cleanly, and I saw no embedded instructions.
